title: Consolation and desolation
hook: moods that draw you toward or away from God

segments.voice: Yesterday, the third and fourth weeks: sorrow, then joy, both on his behalf. Your line was with him in both. Whose good news were you glad for? Day one thousand one hundred forty-six.

Here's a question for any ordinary afternoon: which way am I drifting? Not how am I doing. Not am I happy. Which way. Alongside the Spiritual Exercises, Ignatius of Loyola sets down rules for noticing the movements inside a person. His own account traces them back to the sickbed we met a week ago: the shattered leg, the reading, the daydreaming. Some daydreams left him dry and restless afterward. Others left him content and drawn toward God. So he started paying attention to the aftertaste. Today's word is his name for one of those two pulls: consolation.

Consolation, for Ignatius, is any movement inside that draws a person toward God. He describes it several ways: being set on fire with love of God; tears that move toward love; any growth in faith, hope and love; an inner joy and quiet that pulls toward heavenly things. Desolation is the opposite pull: darkness, restlessness, a tug toward low things, feeling without hope or love, lazy, lukewarm, sad, as if cut off from God. Here's the surprise. Consolation is not the same as feeling good, and desolation is not the same as feeling bad. Ignatius counts tears of grief over one's sins as consolation, because they draw toward God. And a cheerful, busy week can be desolation underneath, if it's quietly drifting away. The test is direction, not temperature. Paul gives a list that works almost like a compass. In the King James words: "But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith." When those are growing, something is moving the right way. Ignatius adds a second detail that's easy to skip. The same feeling can mean different things depending on where a person is heading. For someone sliding toward harm, a nagging unease can be a mercy, a knock on the door. For someone trying to grow toward God, a voice saying what's the point can be the pull away. So he asks people to notice not only the mood, but the arrow under it. And desolation isn't automatically a verdict. Ignatius gives three reasons it comes: sometimes our own slackness, sometimes a testing, sometimes to show that consolation is a gift, not an achievement. It's weather to read, not a sentence passed.

Here's the practice: notice today's drift. Settle and breathe. Run back over the day so far, like a short film. Don't hunt for good or bad moments. Watch for direction. Where did something open you up: toward people, toward patience, toward God, if that's your language? Where did something close you down, pull you inward, make everything feel pointless? Pick one of each. Just name them. If you pray, you can thank God for the first and bring him the second. The bell holds the time.
Consolation. Ignatius' word for any movement inside that draws a person toward God, and toward faith, hope and love, even when it comes with tears.
Your line: which way am I drifting? Today, ask it once at noon and once at night, and notice the arrow, not the mood. Day one thousand one hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: In Ignatian spirituality, people notice consolation and desolation in the daily examen and talk them over with a spiritual director, who helps them read which way the movements are pulling.

fork.setup: a cheerful, busy week, but you've quietly stopped caring about anyone outside your own plans. by Ignatius' test, what is it?
options: possibly desolation: the arrow points away.
fork.reveal: the test is direction, not temperature. a happy surface can sit on top of a drift away.

notes: Paraphrases the First Week rules 1–4: the spirits' different action on those going from bad to worse and from good to better; the descriptions of spiritual consolation (including tears for sins) and desolation. Confirm.
The convalescence story (daydreams of worldly deeds leaving him dry, of imitating saints leaving him content) is from Ignatius' Autobiography; framed as 'tradition says'. Confirm.
Galatians 5:22 quoted in part (the verse continues into 5:23). Confirm the KJV wording.
Original: Latin consolatio; pronunciation given in ecclesiastical style. Confirm; the Exercises were written in Spanish (consolación).

Editor: the hook's sickbed line now points back to day 1139 (which told the convalescence) instead of retelling it as new, and attributes it to his own account (the Autobiography) rather than 'tradition says'.

Auditor: the teach and myth said desolation is 'expected, not shameful' and 'not about blame', which contradicts First Week rule 9, where Ignatius gives three causes of desolation, the first being our own tepidity, sloth or negligence. Rewritten to name all three causes (paraphrased); the myth now says 'always', and its reveal names the three. Confirm against rule 9.
